excerpt: Why sound disappears, how the volume keys actually work, how to use headphones without hurting your ears, and what to check when a video plays silently.

body.text: This lesson explains sound on a computer. You will learn where the volume controls live, how headphones change what you hear, and what to check when a video plays with no sound. If a machine has ever gone silent on you, this is the order to check it in.

Sound has three parts: the program that plays it, the speaker or headphones, and the volume setting for each. A fault in any one of them makes the machine look broken while the other two are working normally.
Before you start

items: A computer with a video or a song you can test with.
Headphones or earphones, if you have them.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Find the volume controls
Most laptops have volume keys on the top row, marked with a speaker and small waves. Pressing one changes the system volume, which applies to everything.

items: Press the volume up key once and look at the screen.
Click the speaker icon at the right of the taskbar to see a slider.
Drag the slider up and play something to test it.
Click the small arrow beside the slider to choose which device plays the sound.
On a Mac, use the volume keys, or the speaker icon in the menu bar.

body.text: You will see a small bar appear on the screen showing the new level, and it fades after a second or two. If the bar has a crossed-out speaker beside it, the sound is muted, and pressing the key again usually brings it back.

body.alt: A laptop keyboard with the volume keys highlighted on the top row.
body.caption: The volume keys change everything at once. The small bar on screen is the confirmation that the press registered.

body.text: It looks like nothing happens when you press the key, because the bar is small and disappears quickly. Watch the same corner of the screen for two seconds before deciding the key is broken.
Program volume and system volume are different
Windows remembers a volume level for each program as well as one for the whole machine. A video can be silent because its own slider is at zero while the system is at eighty.

items: Right-click the speaker icon and choose Open volume mixer.
Look for the program that is playing, such as Chrome or VLC.
Raise that slider, then test the sound again.
Check the mute button inside the video player itself.
Check the volume inside a video call app, which is separate again.

body.text: None of this needs a technician, and the mixer explains most silent videos on a machine that works fine everywhere else.

body.alt: Earphones plugged into a laptop beside a notebook.
body.caption: Plugging in earphones moves the sound to them. If they are faulty, the machine is silent and still correct.

body.text: Headphones, and looking after your ears
Headphones are better than a speaker in a shared room, and they are also a common reason for missing sound, because the machine sends audio to a jack that has nothing in it.

items: Push the plug in fully, until it clicks or stops.
If the sound moves to the earphones, the jack works.
Keep the volume under about sixty percent for long listening.
Take a break every hour, and never raise the volume to drown out a loud room.
Unplug before you put the laptop away, so the cable does not bend inside the jack.

body.text: Do not worry about the tiny buzzing you hear in cheap earphones at high volume. It is usually the earphones, not the computer, and it is a reason to turn the volume down rather than replace the machine.
If it goes wrong
These six cases cover almost every silent computer, and the first two solve most of them.

items: No sound at all: check the speaker icon for a mute symbol, then raise the system slider.
One video is silent: check the player's own volume and mute button.
Sound plays but is very quiet: raise the program slider in the volume mixer.
Sound comes from the wrong device: click the device arrow beside the slider and choose speakers or headphones.
Crackling sound: the plug is half in, or the cable is damaged. Try another pair.
No device is listed at all: restart the computer. If it is still missing, the sound driver needs reinstalling by a technician.

body.text: Practice
Five minutes with the mixer and you will never be confused by a silent video again.

items: Play a song and raise the volume with the keyboard.
Open the volume mixer and lower only that program, then raise it again.
Plug in earphones and watch the device change.
Unplug them and confirm the sound returns to the speakers.
Set the volume to a comfortable level and note the number.

body.text: You can now find the exact place a silent machine lost its sound. In the next lesson you will do the same for the screen, which has its own set of settings.

excerpt: How to set brightness so you can read without strain, why the screen looks different at night, and what to do when the display dims on its own.

body.text: This lesson explains screen brightness and night settings. You will learn the brightness keys, the automatic setting that dims the screen by itself, and how to make a laptop readable in a bright room without straining your eyes.
Brightness is not only comfort. A screen that is too bright in a dark room tires your eyes, and one that is too dim in daylight makes you lean in and squint, which is how headaches start.
If your eyes ache after an hour at the screen, you are not being fussy. Brightness and distance cause most of it, and both are adjustable today.
Most people work at the wrong brightness for months without noticing, so fixing it late is a common and sensible thing to do.
Before you start

items: A laptop or a desktop with a monitor.
The room light you normally work in.
About ten minutes.

body.text: The brightness keys
Look along the top row of the keyboard for a small sun symbol, or a sun with a hollow centre and one with a filled centre. Those are the brightness keys on most laptops.

items: Press the sun-down key once and watch the screen change.
Press the sun-up key to brighten it again.
On Windows, open Settings, then System, then Display, and use the slider.
On a Mac, use the brightness keys, or Control Centre.
On an external monitor, find the buttons on the edge of the screen itself.

body.text: You will see a bar appear in the corner showing the new brightness level, and the screen will change while you hold the key. On a desktop with a separate monitor, the keyboard keys often do nothing, because the monitor has its own controls.

body.alt: A laptop screen at low brightness in a dim room.
body.caption: Brightness is a setting, not a fault. The bar on screen shows the level you have chosen.

body.text: It looks like the screen is failing when it dims and brightens by itself. Most laptops adjust brightness to the light in the room, and the change is the machine following a sensor, not a broken display.
Automatic brightness, and how to stop it
Many laptops have an ambient light sensor near the webcam. It lowers the brightness in a dark room and raises it by a window, which saves battery and annoys people who are trying to read.

items: Open Settings, then System, then Display.
Look for Brightness and a checkbox about changing brightness automatically.
Turn it off if the changes distract you.
On a Mac, open System Settings, then Displays, and switch off automatic brightness.
Battery saver also lowers brightness, so check it when the screen dims suddenly.

body.text: None of this damages the screen. The setting is a preference, and the machine will run happily at any level you choose.

body.alt: A person adjusting a laptop screen in a bright room.
body.caption: Match the screen to the room. A bright screen in a dark room tires the eyes faster than a dim one in daylight.

body.text: Reading at night without strain
At night, the room is dark and the screen is a lamp pointed at your face. Windows and macOS both offer a warm mode that removes some blue light in the evening.

items: On Windows, open Settings, then System, then Display, then Night light.
Set a schedule for sunset to sunrise, or turn it on at a fixed time.
On a Mac, open System Settings, then Displays, then Night Shift.
Lower the brightness a little as well, because the colour change alone is not enough.
Sit about an arm's length from the screen, with the top of it at eye level.

body.text: You will see the screen turn slightly yellow when night light is on. That colour is expected, and it is why photographs edited at night can look too blue the next morning.
If it goes wrong
A screen problem is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, and the first three items solve most of it.

items: The screen is too dark to read: raise brightness with the keys, then check battery saver.
The brightness keys do nothing: the function keys may need Fn held, or a monitor is being used instead.
The screen flickers: change the refresh rate in Display settings, or try another cable.
The picture is yellow all day: night light is on. Turn it off in Settings.
Everything is huge or tiny: that is display scaling, not brightness. Change it under Display, then Scale.
The screen goes black when you move: a loose cable or a failing backlight. Test with another monitor before buying a new machine.

body.text: Practice
Set it once in daylight and once at night, and your eyes will tell you which is right.

items: Find the brightness keys without looking at this page.
Set the screen to a level that is comfortable in your usual room.
Turn automatic brightness off and on, and notice the difference.
Schedule night light for the evening.
Move the laptop so the window is not directly behind it.

body.text: You can now make the screen comfortable in any room, which is the first fix for most eye strain. In the next lesson you will add a second screen without confusing the computer.

excerpt: How to connect a second monitor or a projector, choose between extending and duplicating, and fix the black screen that follows a wrong cable.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to connect a second screen or a projector and choose what appears on it. You will know when to extend and when to duplicate, and what to do when the projector shows nothing at all.
A second screen is either a copy of your laptop screen or an extension of it. That single choice explains most of the confusion: people expect one and get the other, then decide the cable is broken.
Before you start

items: A monitor, television, or projector with its power cable.
The right video cable: HDMI is the most common today.
A laptop or desktop with the matching port.

body.text: Connect and choose
Put the cable in firmly at both ends, then switch the second screen on. A projector often needs a moment to warm up before it shows anything.

items: Plug the cable into the laptop and into the second screen.
Switch the second screen on and choose the correct input, such as HDMI 1.
On Windows, press Windows and P to open the display menu.
Choose Duplicate to show the same picture, or Extend to add a second desktop.
Choose Second screen only when you are presenting and want the audience to see nothing else.
Press Windows and P again to change your mind, at any time.

body.text: You will see a small panel slide out from the right side of the screen with four choices, and the picture change as soon as you pick one. On a Mac, open System Settings, then Displays, and choose Mirror or Extend.

body.alt: A laptop connected to a second monitor on a desk.
body.caption: Duplicate copies the laptop screen. Extend adds a second desktop, and windows can be dragged between them.

body.text: Extend without losing windows
When you extend, the second screen is a separate space. A window can be open on it while your laptop shows something else, and dragging to the edge carries the window across.

items: Open Display settings and drag the two screen boxes to match the real desk.
Check which screen is marked 1, and put it on the correct side.
Move the mouse to the far edge of one screen and keep going to reach the other.
If a window is lost, press Windows and P and choose Duplicate, then move it back.
Set the second screen as the main display if you use it more than the laptop.

body.text: It looks like a lost window has closed. It is usually sitting on the other desktop, and the duplicate trick above brings it home in two seconds.

body.alt: A projector showing a laptop presentation on a wall.
body.caption: A projector is a second screen with a warm-up time. Choose the right input on it before you blame the laptop.

body.text: Presenting without surprises
A room full of people is the wrong place to discover a setting. Two minutes of preparation removes almost every failure.

items: Connect and test before people arrive.
Use Duplicate if you want to see what the room sees.
Use Presenter view if you want notes on your screen and slides on theirs.
Turn off notifications, or switch on Focus assist, so private messages stay private.
Close the tabs you do not want the room to read over your shoulder.
Keep the cable where nobody will trip on it.

body.text: None of this needs a technician, and the first item prevents most of what goes wrong in a hall.
If it goes wrong
A blank second screen is almost always one of these six things, in this order.

items: Nothing appears: check the second screen is switched on and set to the right input.
The laptop does not notice the cable: press Windows and P and choose Extend, then try another cable.
The picture is on the wrong screen: press Windows and P and choose the option you actually want.
The picture is stretched: set the resolution in Display settings to the screen's own resolution.
There is no sound on the television: choose the television as the sound device in the volume menu.
The projector keeps sleeping: move the mouse or press a key, or change its sleep setting in the projector menu.

body.text: Practice
Do this once at home and the next presentation is calm.

items: Connect a second screen and press Windows and P.
Try Duplicate, then Extend, and watch the difference.
Drag a window from one screen to the other.
Move the screen boxes in Display settings to match your desk.
Disconnect and reconnect the cable while the machine is on.

body.text: You can now use two screens without losing a window, and you know what to check when a projector stays dark. In the next lesson you will meet the ports that carry all of this.

excerpt: What the different USB ports are for, how to plug something in without forcing it, why a device charges but does not work, and how to remove it safely.

body.text: This lesson explains USB ports and the devices that use them: keyboards, phones, printers, drives, and chargers. You will learn which port does what, how to plug in without forcing anything, and how to remove a device without losing work.
USB is one connector with several jobs. It can carry data, supply power, or both. That is why one cable can charge a phone and another identical-looking cable cannot move a single file.
Nothing here can break a device. A wrong cable does nothing at all, and a wrong port refuses to accept the plug at all.
Before you start

items: A computer and one USB device you own.
A torch or the phone light, to see the ports at the back.
About ten minutes.

body.text: The shapes, and what they mean
The rectangle you already know is USB-A. The small oval that fits either way up is USB-C. The squarer one on printers is USB-B, and the tiny one on older phones is micro-USB.

items: Look at the port before you look at the plug.
USB-A goes in one way only, with the plastic block facing the right side.
USB-C goes in either way, so never force it.
A blue plastic block inside a USB-A port usually means a faster version.
A port marked with a lightning bolt can charge a device even when the laptop is asleep.
If the plug does not enter with light pressure, it is the wrong shape or the wrong way up.

body.text: You will see the device appear in File Explorer within a few seconds, or hear the short sound Windows plays when it recognises hardware. No sound and no icon means the machine has not seen it, and that is a cable or port question rather than a software one.

body.alt: A row of USB ports of different shapes on a laptop.
body.caption: Look at the shape before you push. A port that needs force is the wrong port.

body.text: Charging but not working
A cable that charges a phone may carry no data at all. Charging needs two wires, and data needs four. Many cheap cables have only the two.

items: Try the cable that came with the device.
Try another port on the computer.
Try another computer, to learn whether the fault is the cable or the machine.
For a phone, choose File transfer on the phone's screen when it asks.
For a printer, install the maker's driver rather than expecting it to work by itself.

body.text: It looks like a device that charges must be working. A phone can charge happily all evening through a cable that will never move a photograph, and that is the most common USB surprise.

body.alt: A keyboard, a flash drive, a phone cable and a printer cable side by side.
body.caption: Four devices, one port family. The cable matters as much as the device.

body.text: Remove a device safely
Removing a drive while it is being written to can leave a file half-saved. The operating system offers a safe way out, and it takes one click.

items: Close any file that is open from the device.
Click the USB icon near the clock and choose Eject.
Wait for the message saying it is safe to remove.
Pull the device out.
On a Mac, drag the drive icon to the bin, which turns into an eject symbol.

body.text: None of this is fussiness. Files that are half-written are the ones people describe as corrupted, and the eject button exists to prevent that.
If it goes wrong
USB problems are usually physical, and the first four checks solve most of them.

items: The device is not recognised: try another port and another cable before anything else.
The plug will not fit: it is the wrong shape, or upside down. Never force it.
The computer says the drive is in use: close the window showing its files and try the eject again.
A phone appears but shows no files: set the phone to File transfer rather than Charging only.
The port feels loose: use another port. A worn port can lose the connection mid-copy.
A device gets very hot: unplug it and let it cool. Do not leave a cheap charger in overnight.

body.text: Practice
Practise with one device you already own, and the shapes will stop being a puzzle.

items: Find every USB port on your machine and count them.
Plug in a flash drive and watch it appear in File Explorer.
Eject it properly and confirm the safe-to-remove message.
Plug in a phone, choose File transfer, and look at its folders.
Try one cable that only charges, and note that no icon appears.

body.text: You can now plug anything in with confidence and remove it without damaging a file. In the next lesson you will fix the silence that follows when the sound has gone missing completely.

excerpt: A step-by-step check for a silent computer, from the mute key to the sound driver, with what each result tells you before you call a technician.

body.text: This lesson is a checklist for a computer with no sound. You will work from the simplest cause to the last one, and know what each result means. By the end you will either have sound back or know exactly which part failed.
Sound fails in order of likelihood: muted somewhere, playing to the wrong device, a loose plug, or a missing driver. Working in that order saves an hour of guessing.
You will see the device name change beside the slider as you test, which is how you know the computer noticed the plug.
Before you start

items: A video or song you know has sound.
Headphones, to test the jack.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: Check these five in order
Do them in this order and stop as soon as the sound returns. Each step rules out one cause for good.

items: Look at the speaker icon in the taskbar. A crossed speaker means muted, so click it once.
Raise the volume slider and play something.
Open the volume mixer and check the program's own slider is not at zero.
Click the device arrow and confirm the speakers or headphones are the chosen output.
Unplug and replug the headphones, then check the device list changed.
Restart the computer, which reconnects the sound device.

body.text: You will see the output device name in the menu beside the slider, such as Speakers (Realtek) or Headphones. If the machine is sending sound to a device that is not plugged in, the room is silent and the computer is behaving correctly.

body.alt: Windows sound settings showing output device options.
body.caption: The output device is the one line to read. Most silent computers are sending sound to an empty jack.

body.text: When the device itself is the problem
If the mixer and the device list look correct, the fault is in the hardware chain: the speaker, the jack, or the driver.

items: Try the headphones in another device, such as a phone.
Try other headphones in the computer.
Try a USB headset, which uses a different path and often works when the jack does not.
Listen for a click when you plug into the jack. Silence may mean a broken socket.
Check Device Manager for a yellow warning sign beside the sound device.

body.text: It looks like the whole computer has failed when one headset does. Speakers and jacks are the cheapest parts and the ones that break first, so test them before you worry about the machine.
Do not worry if you cannot hear a difference between the tests. Write down which combination produced sound, because that single note tells a technician where the fault is.

body.alt: A laptop with a muted speaker icon on the screen.
body.caption: Start with the mute icon. It is the cause more often than any other, and the fastest to check.

body.text: The driver, explained once
A driver is a small program that tells the operating system how to talk to a piece of hardware. If it is missing or damaged, the device disappears from the list entirely.

items: Open Device Manager from the Start menu.
Expand Sound, video and game controllers.
Look for a device with a yellow triangle.
Right-click it and choose Update driver, then search automatically.
If nothing is found, visit the maker's website and download the driver for your model.
Restart after installing, then test the sound again.

body.text: None of these steps damages anything, and the last one is the reason a technician asks for the model number of the machine.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is common in a shared or older machine, and none of them means the computer is finished.

items: Sound works in one program only: the mixer slider for the other program is low or muted.
Sound returns after a restart and goes again: the driver is failing. Reinstall it from the maker's site.
No output devices are listed: the driver is missing, or the audio service is stopped.
Only one earphone plays: the plug is half in, or the earphones are damaged.
A microphone does not work: choose the right input device, then allow microphone access in Settings.
A technician says the board must be replaced: ask for a USB sound adapter first, which costs a fraction and solves a dead jack.

body.text: Practice
Run the whole list once on a working machine, so you know the path before you need it.

items: Mute and unmute the speaker from the taskbar.
Open the volume mixer and find the slider for the program playing.
Plug in headphones and watch the device name change.
Open Device Manager and find the sound devices without changing anything.
Write down the name of your output device, so you can find it again.

body.text: You can now diagnose a silent computer in order instead of guessing. In the next lesson the chapter turns to power, which decides how long any of this keeps working.
